utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everybody in the courtroom. This is case number IT-98-32/1-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution I am Dermot Groome, I am accompanied by Frederic Ossogo, Adam Weber and our case manager today is Sebastian van Hooydonk and we are also assisted by an intern by the name of Solmaz Firoz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And for the Defence of Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Jason Alarid appearing on behalf of Mr. Milan Lukic who is present in Court. I am also present by legal assistant, Maria O'Leary, my case manager, Vladimir Rasic, and another legal assistant, Mihailo Lakcevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're very well resourced, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I think so, thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And for the accused Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Djuro Cepic, Defence counsel for Mr. Sredoje Lukic appearing with me on my left-hand side my learned friend, Mr. Jens Dieckmann, as a co-counsel, behind us on my left-hand side is our legal assistant Ms. Christina Kerll, behind me is our case manager Ms. Sladjana Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We have a busy day ahead of us. We are going to begin with the Pre-Trial Conference. Then there will be a break. Thereafter will follow the opening statements and, if possible, the calling of witnesses. On my list I have several issues to deal with and I begin with the disclosure and translation matters. During the status conference on the 12th of June, the Prosecution informed the Chamber that translations for a number of documents were still pending. May I ask, Mr. Groome, what is the status in relation to these translations?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, all translations now have been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, and since you're on your feet you may as well answer this question. It relates to the photograph spreadsheets that could not be located.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I've stated in prior occasions, the Prosecution cannot find those spreadsheets -- those photo spreads. There is nothing has changed since the last time I reported that to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the consequence of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there are many of the photo spreads have been disclosed with respect to particular witnesses. I recognise to the extent that witnesses are called and the Prosecution is unable to produce the photo spreads that they were shown, that is going to be a matter for the Chamber to consider in assessing the credibility and the reliability of that witness. It is not all witnesses, Your Honour. It is some witnesses that are shown several photo spreads and those photo spreads cannot be located now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any other disclosure matters to be raised by either party? If not, I move to agreed facts. I understand that negotiations are still ongoing and I'd like to find out the status of those negotiations. Mr. Groome and then Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Ossogo has been taking personal charge of this aspect of the case, and I'd ask him to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before we reported before you on February 29th, 2008, the -- what we said to the Defence as regards the possibility of agreeing on a number of facts, we have not received a response from the Defence. We know, however, that they have only admitted four of the facts amongst the 79, and they have indicated that after they completed their investigations, in particular as regards a number of witnesses, they may contact us again. So we have not received any counterproposal on the part of the Defence in order to be able to continue these negotiations. That is the present state of affairs as regards our negotiations. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Alarid?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are still in [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I apologise. Your Honour, we are still in the preliminary stages of investigation still. We've opened an office. We do have a good team in place but as the depth of the trial are kind of still in the distant forest we are really focusing on what's going to start with in the next three days and the continued investigations and our obligations for alibi witnesses and even just exculpatory evidence in general. We will attempt to -- I can see as I'm going through the facts, going through the Vasiljevic transcripts, there are some facts that we would be willing to agree on but I'm not in a position at the point of opening to make those agreements at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, it's a little late to be in a preliminary stage of the trial starting today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I agree with that, and that has been the difficult point of the situation as a total; and I know there has been problems with counsel, those problems with counsel have transcended my entry into this case. As you know, I only came in as co-counsel in -- and was appointed March 10th. I was appointed lead counsel, and I've only been lead counsel for three months. My staff has only been in place for a few weeks and that is the truth of my preparation. I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Alarid. I warned you, however, to move ahead with your work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And we have been, Judge. I'm as ready as I can be to proceed forward today. It's not a matter of lack of diligence. It's simply a matter of the resources available at the time. For instance, Your Honour, our investigator still is not been appointed even though we requested him mid-June and so those are the kind of little things but they are big things when we have been racing to trial in such a manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why has your investigator not been appointed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: It's still with the Registry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, that's a very serious matter, and I'm going to ask the court deputy to bring to the attention of the registrar the failure of the Registry to appoint an investigator for the Defence. It goes to the question of equality of arms and the registry should see that the investigator is appointed as soon as possible so that the Defence can proceed with its investigations. This is normal, and it should be done.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into his microphone when he takes the floor? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I now understand that the matter is in hand and that the Registry is, in fact, proceeding with its own investigations in relation to the candidate, so I expect that that will be dealt with shortly. If it is not, then please bring it to our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I will, sir, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, your microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll say that again. The Prosecution filed a motion on adjudicated facts, both accused persons have objected to the motion, and the Trial Chamber will give its decision in due course. In the motions that have been filed since the last Status Conference, the Defence has consistently -- that's the Defence for Milan Lukic, has consistently requested the Trial Chamber to reconsider the date for the start of trial. Insofar as that is a formal request, I have to say that the Chamber is not at all convinced by the submissions of the Defence and will not reconsider the date for the start of trial. I move next to the question of alibi rebuttal witnesses. The Prosecution has indicated that it intends to call four witnesses to rebut alibi evidence to be led during the Defence case. Following the case law of the Tribunal, these witnesses are to be called during the Prosecution's case in chief. I turn next to the issue of the time for the Prosecution case. The Chamber notes that the Prosecution intends to present the evidence of 50 witnesses during an estimated 69 hours of examination-in-chief. On that matter, I make the following comments: First, the Prosecution estimates one hour for examination-in-chief for the witnesses it intends to call pursuant to Rule 92 ter, but in accordance with the Tribunal practice, 30 minutes will be allowed by the Chamber for these witnesses. If the Prosecution requires more time, then it must make an application to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I address the Chamber on that issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this case is somewhat different than other cases that are before the Tribunal, in that here we have the direct perpetrators of the crimes so in many cases these witnesses, they will be speaking about their observations of the two accused, what the accused did, which is very different than many of the other cases before the Tribunal where that is not the case. The Prosecution put forward its motions for 92 ter because we think that there is great benefit in leading in written form evidence of those witnesses with respect to background information and if that's not directly related to the accused but so much of their evidence is going to be directly related to their observations of the two accused and what they did and their ability to recognise them, that I don't believe that we can do that in 30 minutes. I'm mindful the Chamber's concern of running the case as efficiently as possible, but I don't believe I can adequately lead evidence directly related to the accused in a blanket ruling of 30 minutes. And that's why I, in our filings, had estimated the time that would take to lead the evidence with respect to those witnesses would be an hour. I think we would be able to do it within an hour and use the 92 ter written evidence to deal with all the other evidence not directly related to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us see how we will get on, Mr. Groome, as the case develops. If it is necessary the Chamber will hear an application for more time. The second matter that I wish to raise is that in its filing of the 11th of April, on the 25th of April, the Prosecution limited the evidence of a number of witnesses, five of whom are still included on the witness list, to the matter of alibi rebuttal only. However the summaries of these witnesses indicated that they are also expected to address other matters. The Chamber expects the Prosecution to streamline the evidence of these witnesses so that their testimony is confined to alibi, thereby reducing the time for examination-in-chief, and I'm to say that in principle their evidence should not exceed one hour of examination-in-chief. We have also found examples of cumulative evidence. The Prosecution intends to provide evidence of 15 witnesses addressing the Bikavac incident. 12 of them are to provide their evidence in court, including three witnesses who will provide evidence in rebuttal of the alibi defence. Again, the Trial Chamber expects the Prosecution to streamline the evidence of these witnesses so as to minimise any accumulation of evidence. 20 witnesses are to testify on both acts charged in the indictment, as well as acts not explicitly charged. This is so-called background evidence. Of those 20 witnesses, nine are to testify exclusively in relation to acts not charged in the indictment. Now, the language used in the indictment with respect to the crime of persecutions shows that the crimes with which the accused are charged are those that have been described explicitly in the indictment. The Trial Chamber takes the view that paragraph 4 of the indictment lists the underlying persecutory acts exhaustively, consequently no finding of guilt will be made against the accused for crimes constituting persecutory acts not explicitly listed in the paragraph -- in that paragraph. It is true that evidence regarding non-indicted crimes may be relevant to a number of issues, for example the existence of an armed conflict, the question of a widespread and systematic attack on a civilian population and possibly the issue of discriminatory intents on the parts of the accused, but it does not appear to the Trial Chamber necessary that so many witnesses are called to testify exclusively on these non-indicted crimes. Their evidence will be cumulative to the evidence presented by witnesses called to give evidence regarding the crimes described in the indictment. The Trial Chamber will therefore only allow three of these witnesses to testify. The Prosecution will be allowed to present the evidence of 45 witnesses. Bearing in mind the possibilities for reduction of examination-in-chief that I have just mentioned, it is in the interests of justice that the Prosecution present its evidence within 60 hours. This amount of time reflects the time available for examination-in-chief of the witnesses. Generally each accused will be allowed 60 per cent of the time for examination-in-chief for its cross-examination, but applications may be made for an extension of that time. Allowing some time for procedural and administrative matters, the Prosecution case is expected to conclude on Thursday, the 9th of October. I turn next to pending motions. We have a number of motions, and the decision on those motions will be given in a timely manner. There is, however, one motion that I'd like to mention. It is the Prosecution's sixth motion for protective measures filed on the 27th of July. We could dispose of this matter, Mr. Alarid. We are awaiting a response from Milan Lukic. It is due on the 11th of July, but if you are in a position now or later today to let us know what your position is, it could be disposed of. The Defence of Sredoje Lukic has notified the Chamber that it will not respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We would not be objecting to the protective measures, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 65 ter witness list, the Prosecution has listed a number of witnesses with their full name as well as a pseudonym, but no protective measures have been granted to these witnesses, so I have to ask the Prosecution to clarify whether it intends to apply for those measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would depend upon the specific witness, if I could have an opportunity to review the witnesses that the Chamber specifically referring to, I would be in a position later on today to address the Chamber on which of those witnesses we will be applying for protective measures. There is a motion that we are filing later on today, I'm just reviewing a draft this morning, where we will be seeking protective measures for several additional witnesses, perhaps that will resolve the question that the Chamber is posing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, well, it may very well do that. Thanks. In light of the many changes to the witness list, the Trial Chamber will order the Prosecution to file a new and comprehensive witness list in accordance with the Trial Chamber's decisions on the list. The list is to contain the full names of the witnesses, with the correct spelling. Insofar as witnesses are seeking or have been granted protective measures, this information is to be included in the witness list, including the exact date that such measures were sought or granted. The parties are to provide a list of witnesses every Thursday, and the Chamber will issue a more detailed order in relation to this matter. I want to deal with the notice required in relation to alibi witnesses. This is a matter that concerns you, Mr. Alarid. Rule 67 provides that the Defence must notify the Prosecutor of its intent to offer the defence of alibi. If it does, the notification must specify the place or places at which the accused claims to have been present at the time of the alleged crime and the names and addresses of witnesses and any other evidence upon which the accused intends to rely to establish the alibi. The Prosecution has for some time now been complaining that you have not provided sufficient notice and, indeed, the Pre-Trial Judge has ordered that more specific information be provided. I'm now going to order that the Defence of Milan Lukic provide, by the 18th of July, that's next week Friday, the following information: The place or places at which the accused claims to have been present at the time of the alleged crime, that's the first thing; secondly, the names and addresses of witnesses, that is to say the witnesses whom you intend to call to substantiate the alibi; and thirdly, any other evidence on which you're going to rely to substantiate the alibi. And you are to do this in relation to the following incidents: The Drina River incident the 7th of June 1992; the Varda factory incident of the 10th of June 1992; the Pionirska Street incident, the 14th and 15th of June 1992; the Bikavac incident, the 27th of June 1992; the Uzamnica barracks incident, August 1992 to October 1994; and you're also to provide notice in relation to Mokra Gora. You are to say how that exhibit relates to alibi in relation to the individual incidents alleged in the indictment and also to identify any witnesses that you intend to call in this respect. This is a requirement of the rules. And it is therefore a very good reason. If it is not provided, adverse consequences may flow from that. Mr. Groome, you're on your feet?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there are several matters related to alibi which I must raise with the Chamber. Firstly some of the reasons why the rule is there is not only to give the Prosecution an adequate opportunity to investigate the alibi, but it's also to put the accused on record as to where he is. The Chamber now has ordered that he must provide alibi by notice by July 18th but that puts me in the position now of opening and actually calling a witness to the Drina River incident and giving Mr. Lukic an opportunity hear this testimony, cross-examine this testimony and then after the fact fashion an alibi as to where he was that best conforms to what he believes the Chamber will find credible about this witness. I believe that is manifestly unfair to the Prosecution, and I'm going to request at the very least that the Chamber before I give the opening, ask Mr. Alarid to go into the back with Mr. Lukic and at least with respect to the Drina River, at this stage he must -- he must know where he was, he must know the name of the person who he says he's was with. He's identified him as a Muslim person who he knows. So I'm asking the Court to require him, before I open, before the first witness of the Drina River testifies here today, to at least state on the record where he was, the name of the witness and as much of the information that he has with respect to the witness's address that he has. So at least there is some memorialization of what his case is prior to the taking of evidence. Your Honour, I also wants to address the Chamber with respect to the timing of alibi witnesses. In the conferences we have been told that there are about 50 alibi witnesses that the Defence of Milan Lukic intends to call. The Chamber has just issued an order that all of the alibi evidence must be called by the Prosecution during its direct case and that direct case will be limited to four alibi witnesses and the case will conclude on October 9th. That means that the Prosecution must investigate in excess of the total number of witnesses now the Prosecution is going to be allowed to call in its case in chief, investigate those witnesses and somehow come up with whatever rebuttal prior to the close of our case on October 9th.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Groome is kindly asked to slow down for the translation, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise. I also suggest that that is manifestly unfair. If we are to arrive at the truth at the conclusion of this trial the Prosecution must have a fair opportunity to investigate this alibi thoroughly, the first step is to have adequate notice of it and then the -- is the ability to investigate it and then to call witnesses in rebuttal. The Chamber referred to other cases in the Tribunal with respect to its position that all of the alibi evidence should be called in the Prosecution chief. The one case that I am familiar with, the Vasiljevic case, in which alibi was the central issue, that was not the case, Your Honour. In fact the Prosecution called was permitted to call a significant number of witnesses in rebuttal after it heard the Defence witnesses, and I would suggest to the Court that requiring the Prosecution to call all of its alibi witnesses prior to the calling of the Defence witnesses testifying to alibi puts us in the impossible position of trying to guess at what those witnesses are going to say, attempting to rebut it before it's made and then also gives those witnesses the absolutely unfair advantage of being able to digest all that the Prosecution witnesses have said, identify the gaps in those -- that rebuttal evidence and then craft an alibi testimony that fits neatly within that and I believe that is not going to result in a truthful or accurate fact-finding process and is unfair to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber's decision was actually based on the decision of the Appeals Chamber in Delalic et al where it set the standard for rebuttal evidence. In that case, the Appeals Chamber found that evidence going to a fundamental part of the Prosecution case must be led during the Prosecution's case in chief. And the presence of the accused during the incidents in relation to which a notice of defence of alibi has been entered is a fundamental aspect of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, two matters. First, in relation to the witness, the specific witness, to which the Prosecutor made reference, you would be in a position, would you, to provide the name of that witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we've done better than that and that's why I'm sort of confused at the continuing request of the Prosecution at this point. In a formal pleading, we did not summarise the statements, instead we got notarised statements in Serbian and actually had them translate by my case manager to the best of his ability into English, and we provided both those statements along with the unredacted names. Of course, the statements themselves put the alibi witnesses and Milan Lukic in a place in time so that -- that's why I'm confused as to what specificity do I need to when the statement itself is the best evidence of the information. It is the witness. For Mr. Groome to ask me to go talk to my client and have him disclose these things is basically an affront to an accused's right against testifying against himself because essentially my statements before the Court become my client's testimony before the Tribunal. Instead, we provided the actual witness statements which were notarised and attested to, and I think they are very clear in terms of the time, place and circumstances of their contact with Mr. Milan Lukic in relation to the times of the allegations. I'm really confused as to the reference to Mokra Gora because I had to go back and look at our statements and see if one of the witnesses placed him at Mokra Gora, which I understand is a mountain or a hill top near Visegrad, and we could not find any reference to it so we are not sure if this is just some confusion on the part of the Prosecution, but I didn't find in my materials reference to Mokra Gora.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The legal officer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, as I understand it, Mr. Alarid says he transmitted to you statements from persons and these statements contain all the relevant information that you require.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we are confusing two issues here. The confusing disclosure and notification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please sit, Mr. Alarid, one person on his feet at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Rule 67 talks in very explicit terms about the notification which the Prosecution is entitled to. Yes, on Monday, this past Monday, Mr. Alarid transmitted several statements. I would note that none of those statements, none of those statements, deal with the Drina River so at this stage, the Prosecution has no notification about where Mr. Milan Lukic says he was and who he was with with respect to the Drina River, nor does it have any statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Never mind that. Are you saying, Mr. Alarid, that the Prosecution is in possession of statements which you have transmitted to them, never mind when you transmitted it, whether, under 67 or some other rule, are you saying that they have statements which provide this information? Because I'm looking at the substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If so, well, please identify the date when you supplied that, and they will us what it relates to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour we supplied four statements actually approximately three weeks ago and those were the first four we submitted them as soon as we got them. I believe at least one of those statements did cover the Drina incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You believe?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the statements in front of me, Judge, so in terms of the actual issues, in terms of that, I felt that they covered that week in general of June 7th. Other than that, Your Honour, we've been providing our statements when we have been getting Mr. Rasic and Mr. Lakcevic have been in Bosnia meeting with witnesses. In reference to the 50 names that Mr. Groome ultimately referenced to, those were the 50 names we had achieved with meetings with the client so this still needed follow-up due diligence which we are in the midst of. I can't underscore enough how difficult it is to be preparing a defence when the attorney for multiple murder case has been on board for four months and regardless of Mr. Yatvin's participation, his was primarily 11 bis proceedings and then the attorney-client relationship broke down really for a year going on a year and a half. Then when Mr. Sulejic was appointed, quickly as I got in the relationship broke down; and I think the Trial Chamber is aware of the circumstances and that again provided difficulty because of course an attorney should be present during statements of any witness. And that's where Mr. Lakcevic came in, and we've had him working on it very diligently; but I can't underscore enough that I haven't even interviewed these people personally to basically give the follow-up, I guess, due diligence if you will for the Court's benefit. We are really running as fast as we can. I think we are an at an extreme disadvantage. If the Prosecution claim they are in disadvantage it is only because as we exercise our due process rights we are way behind in this matter and I just don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to give you an opportunity to show to the Court the statements that you say were provided to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which covers the Drina River incident:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, I mentioned earlier that you appear to be well resourced, so have one of your assistants start investigating this matter so that by the time we break, you will be in a position to provide the Court with those statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Judge, just in speaking with Ms. O'Leary as you were conferring with the Chamber, we would be able to do that. We've e-mailed them in PDF format to the Prosecution, as a matter of fact with a note passed to me the two that were delivered actually on Monday deal with the Drina incident, and we could e-mail you the statements in total. It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Groome also raised the question of the time to call the alibi rebuttal witnesses and his submission is that these witnesses should more properly be called after the Defence has presented its case of alibi. I cited an Appeals Chamber decision in Delalic, but I'm bound to say that I'm -- Mr. Groome's submission has some logic to support it. Although Delalic deals with the standard for rebuttal evidence, it may be that what Delalic is speaking about is rebuttal as it is set out, I believe, in Rule -- I think it's 85. It seems to me that Rule 67, dealing with alibi defence, is of its own kind. It is sui generis and when it says the Defence must notify the Prosecutor of the alibi and provide specific information, it appears to me to be only logical that the Prosecutor should rebut that evidence, and normally you rebut evidence after it has been presented, not before. And I'm wondering if Delalic that I have cited actually goes to that point. Delalic speaks of evidence going to a fundamental part of the Prosecution case as being evidence that must be led during the Prosecution's case in chief. But this is not a fundamental part of the Prosecution's case. It only arises as a part of the Prosecution's case because the Defence is raising alibi. Otherwise, the Prosecution would not be dealing with this matter at all, and I'm wondering if Delalic can be distinguished in that way. Are you in a position to assist us, first Mr. Alarid and then Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I understand your point and I think that the root problem of the situation is problems with counsel, the ability to get on the real meat and bones of the investigation at a late start which in terms of course I understand Mr. Groome's position of disadvantage because he feels that he should have been doing this maybe months ago. And on an order of principle, I agree with him. He should have been doing this months ago. But on the same token, with the Trial Chamber's sort of soft start position and the Prosecution's references to our ability to become prepared as the trial proceeds, I think the same argument goes to them. We are not presenting these alibi witnesses in a vacuum, a name and a place, and then we give them no information. We've given them sworn statements so I don't think it's completely relevant to argue that we are going to be able to fashion our alibi after hearing the testimony because in giving a notarised statement, it does limit the wiggle room a witness might have in addressing those kind of concerns of forming the alibi after the fact. We haven't done that. We are really just giving them the information as soon as we get it because we feel disadvantaged but we understand their need to know alibi early because I do agree with Delalic in that the alibi evidence should be presented during the Prosecution's case in chief, the reason being that they should present all evidence of modus operandi the opportunities to commit the crime; and the opportunity to commit a crime if you're talking about a single day then they should have anticipated that, I think they named the witnesses that can show where Mr. Lukic may have been on that day assuming they can prove that; so we are not talking about an extended period of time. I mean, in terms of one of the alibis, if you just want to go towards the Uzamnica barracks, August 92 to together 1994, we can show Mr. Lukic was in prison during a period of time of that extended range; and so if you think about him being in jail, well, that's easy enough recognition but he doesn't need to not present his evidence in a Prosecution case in chief even if we present him with some prison documents which we are attempting to get interest Belgrade right now if we can present those prison documents he does not need to call his Uzamnica barracks witnesses? I think it's important that the Prosecution's case proceeds because it is in the interests of our case that we just get to the end of this, I don't think delay in this point is going to help anybody. If the Court is forcing us to trial as is we are all in the same boat and should proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we want to do the right thing. Can you distinguish Delalic, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think Delalic is talking about a situation where let's say the Defence in the pre-trial brief of the defendant or the accused is that he did not have command responsibility. Well Delalic says okay the Prosecution you knew that prepare that and incorporate that into your -- the presentation of your direct case. Your Honour, at this stage the Prosecution does not even have a proper pre-trial brief from the Defence. It has no pre-trial brief, no alibi Defence, we have -- we are guessing. Case in point. Mr. Alarid has just said that they are looking for jail records with respect to Uzamnica. In all of the filings that have been made related to alibi, as far as I could decipher, there has never been an alibi raised with respect to Uzamnica. Just the other instances which the Chamber has mentioned earlier today. So this is the first time now that I am hearing that an alibi Defence is going to be raised to the last set of charges on the indictment. In terms of a logical, just pure logic, Your Honour, if I were -- I have to prove a negative with the alibi. Witnesses will come, will give sworn evidence about seeing these two men at the times and places related to this indictment. Alibi is very different in that I have to prove that they were not where they say they were. So if they say they were in Obrenovac or they say they were in Belgrade I have to investigate and try to gather evidence that shows that they could not have been there. With respect to the statements that they say were provided, that may tell me where those witnesses say they were, but they do not provide me the information that's clearly, clearly required under Rule 67 and it's very simple information. It's for Mr. Alarid to state on the record after consultation was his client where he says he was, who he says he was with, and the names and addresses of the people he says he's with. It's a notice requirement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're moving now from a position of principle. You now seem to be saying that if you have sufficient information from the Defence on alibi, you would be able to prepare your case and to present it in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I still think the Chamber is -- should not require the Prosecution to provide a rebuttal in the case in chief and I think this one example, I think, may clarify the point. The Defence has no obligation to present a case. We all agree to that. So we could spend, when I finally hopefully get some notification of where Mr. Lukic says he is, if it's 50 witnesses that are going to provide this information, it's conceivable that I could come up with another 50 witnesses to rebut that; so that means in the Prosecution case would be doubled, I would call those witnesses and that at the conclusion of the Prosecution case, Mr. Alarid could make the strategic decision that it's in his clients's best interests not to proceed with the alibi, not to put forward his witnesses. He's under no obligation to do that and not only have we wasted an awful lot of time, but again we haven't gotten any closer to the truth of what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you, regardless of when the Defence is to present -- sorry, when the Prosecutor is to present its rebuttal of the alibi, whether, in chief or following the Defence case, what would your submission be as to the consequence of the failure of the Defence to provide the information that is required by Rule 67?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the remedy is that the Defence can be precluded from introducing that -- the witnesses and introducing the documents that they may seek to rely if they fail to give notification, I think Mr. Lukic always has the opportunity to take the stand and say, I was not there, I was somewhere else. I don't think that that's an appropriate remedy to prohibit that. But clearly, if Defence counsel fail in their obligations to notify about the evidence that they intend to put forward, that the remedy would be precluding. I would also point out Your Honour that yesterday in two decisions that the Chamber has issued, the Chamber has taken the view that the deadline set in the work plan are binding on the parties, and the Chamber has rigorously applied that to the Prosecution with significant impact on the Prosecution case. All of the requirements to provide alibi notice, it's very comparable, there is a great parity between the issues here and have been dictated by a work plan and consistently that work plan has not been met, the deadlines have not been met, and in some cases no extensions were sought. The deadlines came and passed and then the Court in the status conference issued new deadline as the Chamber has done today, issued a new deadline to the Defence of Milan Lukic. It's the Prosecution's position that equality of arms also applies to the Prosecution. That fairness of the trial also applies to the Prosecution. And that it is unfair to require the Prosecution to somehow guess at what the Defence evidence related to alibi is going to be, anticipate it, investigate it and produce it in court under rulings that the Court has made today and limiting us to --or requiring us to conclude the case sometime in the first week in October. I believe that it is manifestly unfair to require the Prosecution to conduct the trial in that way. I think the way to remedy that is to require the Defence to, as soon as possible, and today, before I open, with respect to the Drina, simply state where Mr. Lukic was, who he was with, and as much of the address as he knows. I accept the Chamber's order for the July 18th with respect to the rest of them. The rest of the alibis, but I think before any evidence is called with respect to the Drina River incident, it's imperative that we at least have notification as required under Rule 67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Give us an example as to how you say the Defence will be able to tailor its alibi defence, if you were to open on the Drina before this information is provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: For example, Your Honour, let's say right now there is this kind of vague assertion that Mr. Lukic was not in Visegrad at the time. These crimes occurred late in the day. Let's say the Prosecution was required in our investigations found a witness that said, Well at noon I saw Mr. Lukic in the centre of town having a cup of coffee. I produce that witness, as required by the Court in our direct case, the witness, the Defence witness now in the -- in the --or Mr. Lukic or one of his witnesses, can simply say, "Well, he was there until the morning of the 7th and it was sometime in the afternoon that he left for Belgrade" or Obrenovac or wherever he is now saying he was. It permits the Defence to tailor their evidence to what is introduced during the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. We are going to take a break shortly, but I wanted Mr. Alarid to give us his submissions on the question of the consequence of the failure of the Defence to provide information required by Rule 67. You have heard the Prosecution say that the consequences that you would be precluded from leading that evidence, if you don't provide the required information under Rule 67. That's a very serious consequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, at risk of sounding flip, I think that would be an outrageous remedy because in a totality of the circumstances situation, given the history of counsel, and I think the obvious ability to prepare this case, whether the problems were caused by the client, counsel or a combination, I don't think that there can be any situation that's more difficult on an accused, when you don't get to choose your own attorney. Often times, when I'm hired by a private client, the relationship that I build with that client is essential to the effective preparation of a case and quickly, if the clients is unhappy with me in a private situation, that's easily remedied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, you're making an entirely different points.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, but it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your points relates now to the state of your preparedness. That's not what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, but it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm saying as a matter of law, if the rules require you to provide the Prosecutor with specific information of alibi as to where the accused said he was on a particular day, the names of the witnesses who can substantiate that alibi and any other relevant evidence to substantiate the alibi, what is the consequence of the failure to provide that? Why should you be allowed to lead the evidence? This has nothing to do with the fact that you came into the case late. If you wish to apply for more time in which to provide it, then we can hear that application. But please understand that that is not an answer to the question which I have asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I didn't mean to digress, Judge. I just feel that it is relevant only because when -- I think that I've in good faith provided the information as quick as it's come to me. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so it's been given as quick as I've received it. And I think it is absolutely the most destructive of decisions to exclude evidence because the defendant is always entitled to put on a defence. He may not be required to testify, he may not be required to put on a shred of evidence but he's entitled to put on his defence and if the first time an investigator -- because the contrary is this: Do I go to all my witnesses and say, the first time an investigator from the Milan Lukic team or any team has ever talked to me is June of 2008 related to crimes of 1992 and these are people that had to be located in the mountains in towns they've moved, the same problems the Prosecution had except they've had a dozen years to put this case together, and I've had all of really productive time, eight weeks. And so from an eight week perspective, I mean, I have single victims, single murder cases that take two years that, you know, it takes time to investigate and find the defences and we are doing this all in the confines of eight weeks. And I think that alone from an equity of arms, equality of arms perspective lends at least the tolerance of the Court because at this point in time the Prosecution has really the benefit of all its preparation, to refute us, they have almost unlimited resources on which to contradict our alibi assuming that they feel they have something that contradicts it, they have a lot of staff that can research their files to quickly bring into place someone that says they were drinking with Mr. Milan was drinking coffee at noon that day but in terms of that, like I said, I think the Prosecution would have more of a case had I only given a name, an address and a brief summary. But the fact that I've given sworn notarised statements with facts that place Mr. Lukic in I think a time and place at best as we can at this juncture is more than sufficient at least to preserve the right to put on a Defence because then the alternative is that we would simply be the victims of the accusations of the Prosecutor in a vacuum; and I think there is an absolute risk of injustice if that were to occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the jurisdiction in which you practice when you're not here is there a requirement for notice of alibi?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what is the consequence if that notice is not provided?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: There is a consequence if the alibi was known to counsel and was not timely provided because just in this jurisdiction, the Prosecution is entitled to investigate and coordinate its resources to contradict an alibi if available, so I think the Prosecution in a vacuum is correct in saying that is a possible consequence and so I can't in good faith not concede that; but if an alibi just becomes known to the Defence under the normal course of representation, normally the Court would allow for that if it were in the interests of justice, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're not saying that that is the case here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I do believe it is because there is nothing I've done that is obstructionist at this point, and I think it would be hard for the Court to find even obstructionist behaviour on the part of the clients when you cannot have counsel you can fully comply with at that time. Right now, we've done everything we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The legal officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that the statements to which Mr. Alarid have referred have in fact been provided. They have been provided electronically to the Chamber and to the Prosecutor. We are going to take a break and have a look at those statements, and when we return, we'll give our ruling on the various matters that have arisen. Mr. Groome did you want to say anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one of the statements here, and I was going to point out to the Chamber what I believe Mr. Alarid is referring to but perhaps it's not necessary. The Chamber is going to read the decisions themselves. Your Honour, I just would make the observation that this crime happened 16 years ago. It was one of the first indictments ever issued. Clearly Mr. Alarid in his first interview with Mr. Lukic must have said you say you weren't there, where were you? This whole matter could be resolved in a manner of minutes by simply Mr. Alarid saying, My client says he was here, and he was with these people. It's a very simple matter, but I'll trust the Chamber to revolve it in the way it sees best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are adjourned for half an hour. --- Break taken at 10.12 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I give the Chamber's ruling on two matters. The Chamber reaffirms that it will follow the decision of the Appeals Chamber in Delalic. Accordingly, the Prosecution will lead its alibi rebuttal evidence in-chief. As to the information that has been provided with regard to the first incident, the Drina River, the Chamber has had an opportunity to read some of the statements to which Mr. Alarid made reference. The view that we take is this: The Defence is required to give notice of certain matters. The Defence has proffered certain information. The adequacy, the sufficiency, of that information will ultimately be a matter for the Chamber to decide at the end of the day when it comes to consider whether to accept or reject the defence of alibi. The Chamber, therefore, does not see the evidence provided or any lack of information provided as a ground for precluding the admission of that evidence. As I said before, at the end of the day, the Chamber will evaluate the evidence, and naturally the information that has been provided as to where the accused was or the lack of information that has been provided as to where the accused was and the witnesses to substantiate the alibi will be matters for us to consider. We'll therefore proceed on those bases.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I ask for a clarification, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to the Chamber's order on the 8th of May 2008, directing the Milan Lukic to answer three specific questions, does this order today make that earlier disposition null and void?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You'll have to remind us what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the 8th of May the Chamber directed that with respect to the Drina River incident, that the Defence answer three questions that were put forward in the Prosecution motion. The questions were -- the reading from the decision, the Drina River incidents 7th of June 1992 notice paragraph D as requested in the Prosecution motion paragraphs 15(A) to (C), so they were directed to answer that. Paragraphs 15 A to C read as following: The following clarification is required from the accused. A, where was Milan Lukic at all times on the 7th of June 1992 and with whom? B, what is the name and current postal address of the nominated Muslim witness? C, what other physical or documentary evidence, if any, it is intended that the Defence for Milan Lukic will rely upon to establish this alibi?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, the Defence is still to comply with the information, with the requirement, but the sufficiency of the information is a matter for the Chamber to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, then I apologise for my confusion. Then I don't understand how I can -- how do I -- what do I investigate? I've looked through the statements, there is this vague description that three days after the 4th of June there was a car trip somewhere with some people. We know that the person who gave the statement says that at least some part of that day they were in the car with Milan Lukic. But where does Milan Lukic say he is? That's what I need to investigate. That's only part of what's -- that I'm obliged to investigate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Then your submission will be that the alibi has not been established. That will be your submission when you come to make your submissions. The information which they have provided does not establish alibi. That will be my submission, if I were the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But I must make that the evidence related to the evidentiary basis for that submission must all be dealt with in the Prosecution case before this witness ever arrives to give evidence in the case. So I'm put in the position of guessing about many of the details which, in fairness, the Prosecution must have an opportunity to investigate. And all of that can be cured simply by Mr. Milan Lukic stating, answering the questions that were ordered by the Chamber on the 8th of May and I'm not seeking to have Mr. Lukic himself go on the record. His counsel, as his representative is bound or directed by the order to state that. I'm simply asking that today, before the first Drina witness testifies, that Mr. Alarid state that information on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't understand your difficulty. If I were the Prosecutor, I would consider that I'm in a favourable position. You have nothing to rebut. He has not provided the things which are required by the rules so what is there to rebut? And that would be my submission. But we haven't reached that stage, Mr. Groome. We haven't reached the stage for that submission. As I said, at the end of the day, we have to assess the adequacy or the lack of adequacy of the information provided by the Defence. This is an adversarial system. And you will have a chance to make your submissions on the basis of the information that has been provided by the accused as required by the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I need to make one thing clear. If, of course, the Defence were to provide additional evidence of alibi during its case, I mean, evidence that it has not given notification of, and it is allowed to do that by the rules, then of course the Prosecutor would be entitled, properly entitled, to rebut that after the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, again to clarify, so it's the order of the court that by the 18th of July, the Defence is to provide -- is to comply with the order of the 8th of May providing information and if it doesn't then the Court will take that into consideration when it comes it time to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of course, otherwise we will never start the trial. We'll forever be making orders for them to provide this information as required by the rules. So they must provide it by the 18th as ordered by the Chamber, and if they don't, then the consequences that flow as a matter of law will flow. Now, we were near the end, I believe, of the Pre-Trial Conference, and I am to ask whether any of the accused has anything to say, and I put the question first to Mr. Milan Lukic. Mr. Lukic, do you have anything to say in relation to this? THE ACCUSED MILAN LUKIC: [Interpretation] No, I do not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I put the same question to Mr. Sredoje Lukic. THE ACCUSED SREDOJE LUKIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I also have nothing to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And does any of the -- the counsel have anything additional to add? Yes, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave if we could go to private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There being no other matters to discuss, the Pre-Trial Conference is adjourned. We will resume in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be followed by opening of trial proceedings.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.02 a.m.,
